grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Me levanto; te levantas; se levanta; nos levantamos. Antes de abrir, compartimos el trabajo.

rows: nunca se quedan en el suelo mojado

grammar.note_en:
The small words me, te, se and nos now occur with present verbs such as levantarse, “get up”, and lavarse, “wash oneself”. They identify the participant associated with the action. Elena se lava las manos means “Elena washes her hands”. Yo me lavo las manos means “I wash my hands”; nosotros nos lavamos las manos, “we wash our hands”. With this pattern Spanish normally uses the definite article las before the body part, not a possessive: las manos, not a literal copy of English “my hands”. The person is already identified by me or nos. This is a common way to express care of one’s own body, not a claim that all articles can replace possessives.

A pronominal verb is learned with one of these small person words as part of its pattern. Reflexive here means linked back to the person named as the subject; pronominal is the broader label even when the meaning is not literally doing something to oneself. A finite form identifies person and tense. In these finite present forms, put the small word before the verb: me levanto, “I get up”; te levantas, “you get up”; se levanta, “he/she gets up” or respectful “you get up”; nos levantamos, “we get up”. The verb still agrees with its subject. Nosotros nos is not a duplicated mistake: nosotros names “we”, while nos belongs with the pronominal verb. Ustedes and third-person plural use se, as the plural se quedan in the reading shows. The tables include only person forms actually read; you do not have to supply unseen cells. With negation, no comes before the small word: no se levanta, “does not get up”. In a question the order of these two verb words is retained: ¿Te levantas y te lavas las manos a las cinco? means “Do you get up and wash your hands at five?”. The displayed Spanish contains accents even though the answer checker treats a missing accent as a near miss.

Not every verb with one of these words means a literal action done to oneself. Lavarse las manos has that direct connection; quedarse means “stay/remain”, and ponerse la ropa means “put one’s clothes on”. El gato se queda en el patio means “The cat stays in the courtyard”; los libros nunca se quedan en el suelo mojado means “The books never remain on the wet floor”. A book does not act on itself. Learn the verb with its small word rather than trying to translate every se as “itself”. Sentarse, previously met in se sienta, now also appears in me siento, “I sit down”. This chapter practises finite present forms. It does not require you to attach personal forms to infinitives or commands.

Despertarse, “wake up”, and levantarse, “get up”, are separate events. Elena se despierta at five but initially no se levanta: she wakes but does not immediately rise. Compare me despierto, te despiertas and se despierta with nos despertamos. The stressed singular stem has ie, while the nosotros stem keeps e. Levantarse is regular here: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos. Lavarse follows the regular -ar pattern: me lavo, se lava, nos lavamos. Ponerse has the irregular first-person form me pongo, “I put on”, alongside se pone, “she puts on”, and nos ponemos, “we put on”. The reflexive/pronominal word and the verb ending both identify the person. In the reading the private washing and dressing are done at home; the shared work happens at the patio.

Antes means “before”, después “after/afterwards”. Antes de ir al patio means “before going to the courtyard”; antes de abrir la sala, “before opening the room”. The verb after antes de is an infinitive, with no person ending: ir, abrir, venir. An English -ing translation does not make it a Spanish present participle. With a noun, the same de connection works: después del trabajo, “after the work”, with del = de + el. Used alone, después links events: Después se pone la ropa, “Afterwards she puts her clothes on”. The order matters to the morning routine; one task is not automatically every person’s responsibility.

Siempre means “always”, never a synonym of “early”; nunca means “never”. Nunca leo temprano is “I never read early”, Elena’s description of her old routine at this point. The others’ help creates a new possibility today, rather than proving that an old habit cannot change. The reading places nunca before the verb, so it does not add no in these clauses. Siempre nos ponemos ropa seca means “We always put dry clothes on”. Frequency describes how often an event occurs. Temprano, “early”, places it early relative to an expected time: five is early for a room opening at seven. Pronto, “soon”, means a short time from the reference moment: Pronto llegan Luis y Rosa, “Luis and Rosa will arrive soon”. The English future translation does not introduce a new Spanish future form; the Spanish has the present llegan. Despacio, “slowly”, describes pace, not an early or late time. It can apply to moving a chair, carefully carrying a box, or deliberately reading a letter with pauses. It does not mean someone cannot understand or cannot choose a reading role.

Trabajo here is the work of preparing the room and helping readers, not an assertion about wages or a formal job. Ropa is clothing, normally treated as a feminine singular collective noun: la ropa. A carta is a letter addressed to someone, distinct from the timetable papers or old expenditure account. A firma is a signature, normally a writer’s identifying mark. The new letter names Elena as recipient; its unrecognised cursive mark does not establish who wrote it. 

The reference examples translate as follows: me levanto / te levantas / se levanta / nos levantamos, “I get up / you get up / he or she gets up / we get up”; me lavo las manos / se lava las manos / nos lavamos las manos, “I wash my hands / she washes her hands / we wash our hands”; me pongo la ropa / se pone la ropa / nos ponemos ropa seca, “I put my clothes on / she puts her clothes on / we put dry clothes on”; me quedo aquí / te quedas en la silla / se queda en el patio / nunca se quedan en el suelo mojado, “I stay here / you stay in the chair / stays in the courtyard / never remain on the wet floor”.
